C1.closest: Choi, Zhu & Li (2025), 'Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models?' (arXiv:2508.17536) — majority voting matches or beats decentralized, sparse and centralized MAD across seven benchmarks, with centralized MAD the weakest variant; supported by Smit et al. (arXiv:2311.17371).
C1.just: Choi et al. decompose multi-agent debate and report exactly this ordering on Qwen2.5-7B — majority voting 0.7691 > decentralized MAD 0.7377 (T=2) > centralized MAD 0.6551 (T=2), centralized worst by the widest margin — and prove debate alone cannot raise expected correctness; Smit et al. independently find MAD does not reliably beat simpler protocols. The study's matched-FLOP allowance is a methodological tightening (Choi et al. let debate spend more tokens) and it finds a smaller gap (~4 pts vs ~11 pts), not a new phenomenon.

C10.closest: Kapoor et al., "AI Agents That Matter" (arXiv:2407.01502) — argues agent benchmarks lack cost control and that simple baselines Pareto-dominate complex scaffolds, but flags cost confounds rather than degenerate/duplicate experimental cells. GSO (arXiv:2505.23671) and Tran & Kiela (arXiv:2604.02460) are the nearest empirical evidence that a budget knob can fail to change behaviour.
C10.just: Repeated searches for degenerate factorial cells, duplicate configurations, or cell-collapse audits in agent/orchestration studies returned nothing that quantifies how many nominal experimental cells are physically distinct. The closest literature critiques agent evaluation for conflating cost with capability and for uncontrolled compute, but treats every declared configuration as a real condition; no prior work reports a count like 59 nominal cells -> 41 compute vectors / 38 correctness vectors, or identifies team-size cells that are the same episode.

C11.closest: Huang et al., "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet" (arXiv:2310.01798, ICLR 2024) — debate/self-correction loses to self-consistency at matched response counts; ParaThinker (arXiv:2509.04475) makes the width-over-depth claim explicitly at matched budget.
C11.just: Huang et al. (ICLR 2024) already show multi-agent debate underperforms plain self-consistency at an equivalent number of responses and that intrinsic self-correction without external feedback degrades accuracy; ParaThinker states directly that "scaling compute in parallel (width) is a more effective and efficient way to superior reasoning than simply scaling sequentially (depth)"; Bertalanic & Fortuna (Qwen2.5-7B/Llama-3.1-8B) find debate costs 2.1-3.4x the tokens for equal or lower accuracy; Jwalapuram et al. find automatic MAS underperform CoT-SC at up to 10x cost. Note the boundary condition: Snell et al. find sequential revision *can* beat parallel at matched budget on easy questions when a trained revision model and a verifier are available — conditions absent here.

C12.closest: Brown et al., "Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling" (arXiv:2407.21787), which states outright that selection methods fail to track coverage in domains without automatic verifiers; Qi et al. (arXiv:2506.09014) report the matching oracle-minus-selected table.
C12.just: The coverage/selection gap under repeated sampling is the central result of Brown et al. 2024, who show coverage scales with samples while "common methods for picking from a sample collection (majority voting and reward models) plateau"; Qi et al. 2025 quantify the same gap directly (pass@5 59.74% vs majority vote 49.67% averaged over five math benchmarks), and Stroebl et al. 2024 give the theoretical bound. The study's numbers (oracle 0.542 vs delivered 0.328) reproduce this in a new model/benchmark pairing but establish no new phenomenon.

C13.closest: Liu, "LLMs as a Jury: Cross-Model Consensus Can Outperform Process Reward Models for LLM Reasoning" (arXiv:2607.10139) — same-checkpoint self-judging captures essentially none of the selection headroom; Zhang et al. (arXiv:2608.07813) and Landesberg (arXiv:2603.12520) report the same for pointwise judges.
C13.just: That a model scoring its own candidates adds essentially nothing is established: Liu 2026 finds a single-model self-verifier is "the weakest of the selectors" tested, capturing ~0% of the achievable gain over self-consistency on AIME-2024 and scoring *below* self-consistency on all four benchmarks, and Zhang et al. 2026 measure an unconstrained scalar judge at +1.0 pp over majority vote on GSM8K (10 pts worse on a held-out split). The small plurality-over-random margin is likewise consistent with prior hard-benchmark results (Qi et al. put majority vote ~4 pts over pass@1; Bahuguna 2026 finds majority vote is net negative on most GPQA Diamond items for small models).

C14.closest: Jiang, Yi & Zhu, "Semantic Voting: Execution-Grounded Consensus for LLM Code Generation" (arXiv:2605.08680) — 18 configurations showing output-pattern voting is 18-52 pp behind every execution-based selector, framing selection as a signal-quality problem, but with no quantification of singleton pools or failure decomposition.
C14.just: That syntactic/textual grouping of programs is the wrong equivalence relation is long-settled — AlphaCode and CodeT both cluster by execution behaviour for exactly this reason, and Jiang et al. 2026 measure execution-based selectors beating output-pattern majority voting by 19-52 pp — but no retrieved work quantifies the failure structure itself. Jiang et al. explicitly document the no-survivor failure only qualitatively; none report singleton-pool prevalence (144/200), a structural-vs-stochastic split of failures (77%), or a wrong-pick rate conditional on correct programs being the majority (6-8%). Caveat: AST-canonical grouping is a known-weak baseline, so the claim reads as an accounting of a baseline the field has already abandoned rather than a new defect.

C15.closest: Cai, Kulik & Choudhury, "ARBITER: Reasoning Trajectory Basins and Majority Vote Failures in Test-Time Sampling" (arXiv:2605.26172); Bahuguna, "When Self-Consistency Backfires" (arXiv:2608.11403) for the confidently-wrong-consensus regime.
C15.just: Cai et al. 2026 name and characterise exactly this failure — sampled trajectories collapse into "reasoning basins" and "the correct answer can appear in the pool yet lose to a larger wrong basin", with worked cases of a 4-sample correct challenger losing to an 18-sample wrong dominant basin — and Bahuguna 2026 shows the wrong-consensus regime dominates on hard science questions (majority vote lowers per-problem accuracy on 56.6%/65.7% of GPQA Diamond items). The study's 91% prevalence and 2-vs-27 median class sizes are a sharper quantification on a harder exam, not a new effect.

C16.closest: Taubenfeld et al., "Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs" (arXiv:2502.06233, Findings of ACL 2025) — same selectors, same ~0.4-1.6 pt band, and the explicit within-question-discrimination diagnosis of why verbalized confidence fails.
C16.just: The magnitude matches prior work almost exactly: CISC reports confidence-weighted voting gains of only 0.4-1.6 accuracy points over plain self-consistency across nine models, and introduces "within-question discrimination" precisely because verbalized confidence is near-constant across a question's own candidates while calibrating only across questions; HLE's own 81-93% RMS calibration errors say stated confidence is uninformative on this benchmark family. Note the interpretive gap: CISC and DeepConf treat that same ~1-point band as a real (compute-saving) signal, and both find logprob-derived confidence — not stated confidence — is the signal that works, so "no usable selection signal" is stronger than the retrieved evidence supports for confidence generally.

C17.closest: Taubenfeld et al. (2025), 'Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs' (ACL Findings), which defines Within-Question Discrimination and shows verbalized confidence is best on between-question calibration metrics and worst within-question; plus Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026), which measures the same near-zero within-item confidence-correctness association across sibling agents.
C17.just: Both halves are established. Taubenfeld et al. introduce Within-Question Discrimination precisely because verbal confidence gets the best between-question ECE/Brier while sitting near chance within a question (Verbal Binary 52.2%, Verbal 0-100 56.1% vs 50% chance); Bertalanic & Fortuna report 31.3-83.7pp overconfidence gaps and a near-zero point-biserial confidence-correctness correlation (r=0.024-0.166) across 10 sibling agents answering the same item, with 78.5-95.6% of scores pinned at the maximum. The 45-62pp gap and the flat within-pool AUC land squarely inside those existing ranges; Qwen3/HLE/BCB is a new substrate, not a new phenomenon.

C18.closest: Nechepurenko & Shuvalov (2026), 'Coordination as an Architectural Layer for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems' - matched-budget Brier plus reliability/resolution across independent, orchestrator, peer-critique and consensus topologies, reproducing the same rank order; Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026) for the certainty-inflation-without-accuracy-gain result.
C18.just: Bertalanic & Fortuna show peer exchange inflates confidence uniformly regardless of correctness and shrinks the correct-vs-wrong confidence gap relative to isolated agents, at equal or lower accuracy; Nechepurenko & Shuvalov, holding tools/context/token budget fixed and varying only topology, report exactly the ordering claimed here (independent ensemble Brier 0.159 < orchestrator-specialist 0.162 < peer-critique debate 0.170 < consensus alignment 0.181) with a Murphy reliability/resolution decomposition. Only one element is not already in the literature: that a single agent merely carrying its own history is the worst-calibrated arm of all, which prior work attributes to social conformity rather than context accumulation.

C19.closest: Shi et al. (2026), 'Confidence Laundering in Agent Systems' - defines uncertain-decision handoff and confidence laundering as exactly this failure mode, but is a position paper proposing latent uncertainty carriers and reports no experiment establishing verbatim confidence reproduction or its scoring consequences.
C19.just: The second half replicates known results - Spiess et al. report Brier Skill Scores of -0.24 to -2.72 for reflective/verbalized confidence against an always-predict-base-rate reference, i.e. strictly worse than a constant, and near-zero within-item resolution follows from Bertalanic & Fortuna's r_pb ~ 0. The first half does not: 896/896 exact verbatim reproduction of the selected candidate's stated confidence by a nominally independent forecast channel is a total degeneracy that no retrieved paper measures. Shi et al. name this mechanism ('confidence laundering': downstream agents inherit the commitment without the uncertainty) but it is a position paper with no measurement, and Paleka et al. only flag the analogous risk that forecasters copy market probabilities from training data.

C2.closest: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026), 'The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate' (arXiv:2605.00914) — sycophantic conformity (85.5% modal adoption), consensus collapse with a 32.3pp oracle gap, and debate-degraded confidence discrimination; corroborated by Zhu et al. (arXiv:2601.19921) and Hao et al. (arXiv:2606.00820).
C2.just: Bertalanic & Fortuna report every component of this claim in the same experiment: debate inflates consensus over isolated self-correction (90.1% vs 81.7% on MMLU-Hard), oracle/pool coverage peaks then falls in later rounds (66.3% at R2 -> 64.5% at R3; Ministral collapsing to 53.0%), and debate shrinks the confidence gap between correct and incorrect answers to +1.4pp (vs +4.2pp under self-correction) on top of extreme miscalibration (98.1 mean confidence at 14.4% agent accuracy). The study's eight-round trajectories sharpen the resolution but not the finding.

C20.closest: Spiess et al. (2025, ICSE), 'Calibration and Correctness of Language Models for Code' - shows verbalized/reflective confidence has strongly negative Brier Skill Score against a base-rate reference and that standard Platt rescaling cuts ECE from 0.32 to 0.03; Shen et al. (ICML 2024) generalize post-hoc calibration to unseen LLM tasks.
C20.just: That a held-out-fitted post-hoc calibrator dominates raw LLM-stated confidence is well established, including on code, one of this study's two benchmarks: Spiess et al. apply Platt scaling to code-LLM confidence and report ECE falling from an average 0.32 to 0.03 (0.38 to 0.05 on the usable subset), and Campos et al. report multicalibration lifting Brier Skill Score by up to +1.03 over uncalibrated confidence. Thermometer establishes the same for held-out tasks with a learned auxiliary calibrator. The 0.491 -> 0.216 magnitude is a new datapoint, not a new finding.

C21.closest: Brown et al. 2024, "Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling" (arXiv:2407.21787), Fig. 4 and the FLOP-rescaling section — 8B dominates 70B at matched FLOPs on math/proof, 70B wins on code. Wunderlich et al. 2026 (arXiv:2605.01566) is the closest compute-matched *orchestration* sweep and disagrees.
C21.just: Brown et al. (2024) already establish both halves within a single dense family at fixed inference FLOPs: Llama-3-8B-Instruct always beats the far larger 70B on MiniF2F/GSM8K/MATH, while for CodeContests "the 70B model is almost always more cost effective" — i.e. the same code-vs-non-code reversal of the size ordering, summarised as "the ideal model size depends on the task, compute budget, and coverage requirements". Only the vehicle is new (final-answer accuracy under five orchestration policies rather than oracle coverage under repeated sampling), and even the compute-matched orchestration sweep has a precedent that reports the opposite sign (Wunderlich et al. 2026: Llama-3.1-70B with plain CoT beats every compute-matched 8B self-consistency/debate/MoA configuration on MMLU-Pro), so the study lands on one side of an already-split literature rather than opening it.

C22.closest: Barzelay et al. 2026, "VAREX: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal Structured Extraction from Documents" (arXiv:2603.15118); plus Neveditsin et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.01810) for the size-stratified parseability numbers and Tam et al. 2024 (EMNLP Industry) for format-restriction cost.
C22.just: VAREX states the claim almost verbatim for the same size threshold — "below 4B parameters, structured output compliance -- not extraction capability -- is a dominant bottleneck" — with schema-echo alone costing 45–65 pp; Neveditsin et al. (2025) report parseability of 80.9% (3–4B) / 82.6% (8B) / 90.3% (14B), numerically very close to this study's 67% vs 80–83% split. The genuinely incremental piece is only the downstream consequence (thinner candidate pools at matched oracle coverage inside a multi-agent aggregation), and one caveat should be noted: Neveditsin et al. attribute small-model loss chiefly to degenerate repetition rather than format per se, so the mechanical/cognitive dichotomy is less clean than the claim asserts.

C23.closest: Tao et al. 2025, "Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of Large Language Models" (arXiv:2505.23854) — same Qwen3 0.6B–32B ladder, opposite scale trend in calibration; Xiong et al. 2024 (ICLR) reports the same positive scale–calibration relation.
C23.just: Tao et al. (2025) run the same family and range (Qwen3 0.6B–32B) with numerical verbalized uncertainty and report the opposite direction: Qwen3-14B and 32B "consistently outperform their smaller counterparts" on both ECE and AUROC, with 8B merely competitive, and Xiong et al. (2024) likewise find calibration improves as capability scales. The disagreement is plausibly regime-driven rather than an error — at HLE's near-floor accuracy scale buys no accuracy, so the hard–easy effect documented by Michael et al. (2026) leaves the largest model with the widest confidence–accuracy gap — but the study must argue that explicitly rather than state the scale trend as general.

C24.closest: Dai & Wang 2026, "Rescaling Confidence: What Scale Design Reveals About LLM Metacognition" (arXiv:2603.09309) — round-number anchoring incl. 50, but across six frontier/large models with no 4B–32B breakdown and no abstention test; Shen 2026 (arXiv:2608.05064) for the 0.5 floor in 0.5B–14B models.
C24.just: Round-number anchoring of verbalized confidence is established — Dai & Wang (2026) show the top three values absorb 78–92% of responses and name 50 as a prominent internal anchor, and Shen (2026) shows small instruction-tuned models' stated confidence rarely drops below one half — but no retrieved work resolves the 0.50 mode by parameter count (59% at 8B, 42% at 4B, 13% at 14B, 0.8% at 32B) or tests whether it carries information. The informativeness half is the real contribution and it cuts against the nearest evidence: Ferdous (2026) finds small-model verbalized confidence detects its own errors at chance (AUROC ≈0.50) while internal token probability reaches 0.92–0.99, so an abstention reading needs a stated discrimination statistic, not just a correlation with correctness.

C25.closest: Patel, 'Representational Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Committees: Measurement and Diversity-Aware Consensus' (arXiv:2604.03809) — effective rank ~2.17/3 for three role-conditioned agents on GSM8K/MATH-500, measured on nomic-embed-text embeddings of rationales, N=3, no code benchmark, no paired no-peer baseline.
C25.just: Patel (2604.03809) already reports that multi-agent committees collapse to an effective rank of ~2.17 out of 3 with mean cosine 0.888, and Chen et al. (2604.18005) attribute diversity collapse to interaction structure itself — so 'orchestration contracts the space agents span' is established. This study moves the measurement from sentence-embedding space into the model's own residual stream, adds a paired independent-vs-peer-exposed contrast on matched items, and replicates it at three depths and in two domains, which is a materially new measurement regime rather than a new phenomenon.

C26.closest: Zhang & Lin, 'Simulated Adoption: Decoupling Magnitude and Direction in LLM In-Context Conflict Resolution' (arXiv:2602.04918) — radial/angular decomposition of hidden states on Qwen-3-4B and others, finds 'Orthogonal Interference' (rotation without magnitude suppression), but single-model knowledge conflict, no inter-agent distances, no dimensionality metric.
C26.just: The methodological half is well established: cosine/scale-free geometry is known to be brittle and to license wrong conclusions (Steck et al. 2024; Rudman et al. 2022), transformer states are known to be anisotropic (Ethayarajh 2019), and Zhang & Lin (2602.04918) already decompose residual-stream updates into radial and angular components under in-context conflict and find magnitude preserved while direction rotates. What is new is the specific cross-agent dissociation — identical mean pairwise distance (52.57 vs 52.50) with a 29% closer nearest pair, 9% farther pair, and 17% higher angular dispersion — which no prior work reports for a multi-agent orchestration contrast.

C27.closest: Wang, Isola & Cheung, 'The Truth Lies Somewhere in the Middle (of the Generated Tokens)' (arXiv:2605.09969) — establishes position-dependence of hidden-state semantic content across generation, but for a single unmanipulated model, with kernel alignment rather than dimensionality, and no orchestration contrast.
C27.just: Prior work establishes that representation quality varies systematically with generation position (Wang, Isola & Cheung: generated tokens beat prompt tokens, mid-generation pooling is richest) and that trajectory geometry evolves over turns, but none crosses an orchestration manipulation with generation-position anchors. The specific finding that peer exposure leaves mid-generation geometry indistinguishable, reverses ordering at the prompt, and reshapes only the committed answer state has no prior analogue I could retrieve.

C28.closest: Ontalvilla, Azkune & Ormazabal, 'Agreement in Representation Space for Open-Ended Self-Consistency' (arXiv:2606.12003) — treats consistency as geometric concentration of sampled generations in embedding space (math, code, summarization), but uses external sentence embeddings, does not separate dispersion from dimensionality, and conditions on reliability rather than token-level unanimity.
C28.just: The closest prior reads agreement as spatial concentration — Ontalvilla et al. cluster generations in embedding space and find central, concentrated generations more reliable — and hidden-state-consistency work treats correct consensus as higher mean pairwise cosine similarity; neither measures the dispersion-times-dimensionality signature this claim reports, and both point the opposite way on the dispersion axis. Zhang et al. decompose wrong-consensus agreement statistically with no geometry at all, so the joint 'more dispersed along fewer directions' result stands unestablished and in tension with the concentration reading.

C29.closest: Parupudi, 'Anisotropy Decides Cosine vs. Rank Metrics for Text Embeddings' (arXiv:2606.29571) — shows metric choice changes conclusions as a function of embedding anisotropy across nineteen encoders and seven datasets, but for retrieval/similarity benchmarks, not multi-agent consensus, and not contrasting code against exam-style text.
C29.just: Parupudi (2606.29571) already establishes the general principle empirically — embedding anisotropy determines whether cosine or non-scale-free metrics recover signal, with the dominant-direction variance fraction predicting the gap at r=0.95 across nineteen encoders — and Steck et al. make the analytic case that cosine can be arbitrary. The new content is the domain-specific instantiation: on BigCodeBench the scale-free metric is empty while the raw norm carries consensus at rho=+0.389, which turns a retrieval-metric caveat into a concrete measurement hazard for multi-agent code studies.

C3.closest: Hussain & Nielbo (2026), 'Conformity Mitigations in Large Language Models Lie on a Single Resistance-Receptivity Frontier' (arXiv:2608.11247); with Weng et al. (ICLR 2025, arXiv:2501.13381) and Zhu et al. (ACL 2025, arXiv:2410.12428) establishing that conformity rises monotonically with majority size.
C3.just: Hussain & Nielbo measure precisely the lone-correct-agent reversal under a unanimous wrong peer group with a clean dose-response in group size (11.2% at one peer -> 22.8% at four on MMLU; 54.8% GPQA; 71.0% SimpleQA), and show 84-89% of reversed answers match the peers' answer verbatim — i.e. the flip is copying, not reconsideration. Their resistance-receptivity frontier is the same asymmetry as the study's 'fixed only when a correct peer exists' decomposition, and Bertalanic & Fortuna's 70% contextual-fragility rate plus '96% of self-correction-only wins had a correct agent at R1' cover the same ground.

C30.closest: Sun & Kazakov (2026), Tool-Call Dependency Structure is Linearly Decodable in LLM Agent Residual Streams (arXiv:2605.25310) — an edge probe on Qwen3-32B's residual stream decodes the abstract tool-call dependency topology well above a Hewitt-Liang random-label control and a positional baseline, with counterfactual contrasts showing it tracks topology not identifier values; paired with Leong (2026, arXiv:2608.28502), where source-format/provenance features probe at 97.5-100% across four models while behaviour does not follow, and Cencerrado et al. (2025, arXiv:2509.10625), where question-only probes already carry most of the correctness signal (0.68-0.88 AUROC, near chance on reasoning).
C30.just: Both halves of the dissociation are separately established: abstract orchestration/pipeline structure is already known to be near-ceiling linearly decodable from a reader model's residual stream (tool-call dependency graphs from Qwen3-32B; source-format provenance at 97.5-100% balanced accuracy; 100-way source-model attribution from a frozen proxy LLM), and correctness probes are known to be weak and to ride mostly on item difficulty rather than answer-specific evidence. The new regime is the label and the artifact: which of three orchestration policies compiled a multi-agent handoff report, read off the same representation that yields only 0.694 AUC for correctness, with an explicit question-only decomposition (0.649 of 0.694).

C31.closest: Lugoloobi et al. (2026), LLMs Encode Their Failures: Predicting Success from Pre-Generation Activations (arXiv:2602.09924) — linear probes on pre-generation activations predict policy-specific success on math and code, beat surface features, and separate model-specific from human difficulty; Di Cicco (2026, arXiv:2606.14530) reports AUC 0.881+/-0.008 pre-generation on Qwen3-4B/LiveCodeBench, and Ruan et al. (2026, arXiv:2607.06503) predict agent-episode failure from first-round hidden states.
C31.just: That per-item difficulty and first-attempt success are linearly readable from the last prompt token before any generation is by now a standard result, demonstrated with stronger numbers than this study's rho=0.29 / 0.66 AUC — 0.881 held-out AUC on LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-4B, rho 0.40-0.64 against model-derived difficulty and AUROC > 0.7 for success under fixed decoding, and a dedicated value-function estimator of LLM-perceived difficulty. The multi-agent framing (will a hub episode succeed) is the only new element, and hidden-state probes predicting eventual LLM-agent episode failure from the first round are also already published.

C32.closest: Wang, Hong & Bagci (2026), A decodability criterion predicts when hidden-state selection beats majority voting in LLMs (arXiv:2608.17124, Information Fusion) — defines within-question AUC on answer-token states, reports 0.51-0.59 for general-purpose models, and shows selection only beats voting above ~0.60; plus Ashuach et al. (2026, arXiv:2604.12373), which shows agreement/consensus structure is what probes actually read.
C32.just: The first half is an almost exact numerical match to CASE, which trains a linear gate on answer-token hidden states and reports within-question ranking AUC of 0.51-0.59 for general models (Qwen, Llama) under question-grouped cross-validation — the same near-chance regime as the study's 0.54-0.63 exam / 0.49-0.54 code. The second half — consensus membership being more decodable than truth — is the explicit finding of Masked by Consensus, where probes exploit shared inter-model agreement patterns rather than correctness, and self-probe advantage only appears once disagreement subsets isolate it.

C33.closest: Kumaran et al. (2026), How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence (arXiv:2603.17839) — traces the information flow on Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 2.5 7B and Magistral Small 24B and finds confidence is gathered from answer tokens and cached post-answer, not tracked during generation; Miao & Ungar (2026, arXiv:2603.25052) add that accuracy and verbalized-confidence directions are near-orthogonal (cosine < 0.04).
C33.just: Kumaran et al. establish exactly this, and causally rather than by decodability alone: confidence representations do not exist during answer generation, they emerge at answer-adjacent positions, are cached at the first post-answer position, and are retrieved at the verbalization site, shown by steering, patching, noising, swap and attention-blocking experiments. Podolak & Verma independently show the verbal score is a statistic of alternatives surfaced during reasoning, i.e. only trustworthy after exploration completes — the same commit-time picture the study infers from R2=0.10 and within-item rho=0.02 at 128/512 tokens.

C34.closest: Chen et al. (2024), Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards Scaling Laws of Compound Inference Systems (arXiv:2403.02419) — proves and measures that query-difficulty diversity drives non-monotone Vote/Filter-Vote scaling because easy and hard queries move in opposite directions; complemented by Yang et al. (2025, arXiv:2505.22960) on debate helping only as difficulty rises, and Haupt et al. (2026, arXiv:2605.30916) on aggregation over heterogeneous items diluting effects.
C34.just: The mechanism is Chen et al.'s: within-task diversity of query difficulty makes aggregation help easy items and hurt hard ones, so pooled curves are non-monotone and pooled means misstate conditional effects; difficulty as the moderator of multi-agent debate is likewise established, and IRT audits already report that benchmarks are dominated by universally-easy and universally-hard items with only a minority discriminating (e.g. 23.8% / 8.4% / 66.8%). What is new here is the quantification under a matched-FLOP crossed design: the specific (0.3,0.7] contested band, the ~4x understatement factor, and the collapse of cross-policy agreement from phi=0.73 pooled to 0.09 inside the band.

C4.closest: Choi, Zhu & Li (2025), arXiv:2508.17536 — flat per-round agent accuracy with majority voting capturing the whole gain; plus Smit et al. (arXiv:2311.17371) and Liu et al. (arXiv:2409.14051) on round-count cost/benefit.
C4.just: Choi et al. show mean agent accuracy is essentially flat (martingale) across debate rounds at T=2,3,5 while consensus tightens, and prove debate contributes no expected-correctness gain beyond the initial ensemble; Smit et al. find no reliable round-scaling benefit, and the token-cost blowup with rounds is quantified in the efficiency line (GroupDebate). The study's extension to eight rounds with an explicit 4.3x FLOP price tag is a more precise accounting of an already-established diminishing-returns result, though note Bertalanic & Fortuna do report continued R1->R3 accuracy gains on GSM-Hard (39.7% -> 56.1%), so 'round 1 delivers the entire gain' is regime-dependent.

C5.closest: Bertalanic & Fortuna (2026), arXiv:2605.00914 — explicit debate vs noise vs self-correction ablation showing peer content is inert and self-correction is not; Hao et al. (arXiv:2606.00820) for the 37% self-reflection flip rate; Huang et al. (ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.01798) for the compatible half.
C5.just: The decisive control runs the other way in prior work: Bertalanic & Fortuna execute the same three-arm ablation (peer debate / noise-injected irrelevant rationales / isolated self-correction) and find self-correction matches or beats debate (54.0% vs 56.1% at R3 on GSM-Hard; 5.9x more items solved by self-correction alone for Ministral) while the noise arm reaches 55.1%, concluding 'task-relevant peer rationales provide no measurable benefit over task-irrelevant ones' — the opposite of 'peer content is the active ingredient'. Hao et al. further report 37% of agent-question observations flip under self-reflection alone, roughly 4x the study's 8.5%; only the weak reading (intrinsic self-correction does not improve reasoning, Huang et al.) survives as replication.

C6.closest: Brown et al. (2024), 'Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling' (arXiv:2407.21787); with Li et al. (TMLR 2024, arXiv:2402.05120) for the slower voted-accuracy curve under the same sampling-and-voting scheme.
C6.just: Brown et al. established exactly this asymmetry: coverage (any sample correct) scales log-linearly over four orders of magnitude while 'majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples and fail to fully scale with the sample budget'. The size of the unconverted headroom has since been quantified as a 32.3pp oracle gap (Bertalanic & Fortuna) and a correct minority in ~1 of 4 divergent cases (He et al.); swapping sample count for team size N at matched FLOPs re-measures rather than extends this.

C7.closest: Cemri et al. (2025), 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (arXiv:2503.13657) — MAST taxonomy over 1,600+ traces, with single-agent setups sometimes outperforming the multi-agent version; and Gao et al. (2026), 'DecisionBench' (arXiv:2605.19099) on emergent-delegation shortfalls.
C7.just: Prior work establishes the endpoint — supervisor/centralized MAS collapsing toward single-agent performance, and orchestrators delegating badly (routing fidelity-at-1 of only 7.5-29.5%, with perfect delegation 15-31pp above measured performance) — but nothing retrieved measures a hub's delegation rate (4.3% of episodes) or identifies output-cap truncation as the dominant hub error (75.5%) driving a self-reinforcing re-prompt loop (74% continuation) with monotonically escalating reasoning length (3,690 -> 7,139 tokens). MAST's 14 failure modes are hand-annotated over traces and include termination/design faults but do not instrument this mechanism per call.

C8.closest: Brown et al., "Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling" (arXiv:2407.21787) — coverage scales log-linearly with samples while majority voting and reward-model selection plateau; the identical claim at far larger k.
C8.just: Brown et al. establish exactly this: coverage (pass@k) scales log-linearly over four orders of magnitude while "majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples and fail to fully scale with the sample budget." Stroebl et al. give the theoretical ceiling (imperfect verifiers bound resampling gains regardless of budget) and Landesberg shows the same failure for pointwise LLM judges in best-of-N (judge recovers only 21% of oracle-selection gain, 67% tie rate). The study's k range (1-10) is three orders of magnitude narrower than Brown's, so the Qwen3/HLE/BigCodeBench instantiation is a benchmark swap rather than a new regime.

C9.closest: Shetty et al., "GSO: Challenging Software Optimization Tasks for Evaluating SWE-Agents" (arXiv:2505.23671), §5.3 "Agents Mismanage Compute" — agents systematically terminate far below the step allowance; and Tran & Kiela (arXiv:2604.02460) App. G on thinking budgets not binding. Neither shows budget levels collapsing to identical episodes.
C9.just: That nominal compute budgets go unspent is documented — GSO reports "even with larger budgets of 200+ steps, 75% of trajectories terminate before 100 steps", Tran & Kiela find visible thought "tends to plateau well below the requested budget" with 1000/2000-token settings already close to 5000/10000, and s1 exists precisely because models will not spend a budget unless forced. What is new is the design-level consequence measured here: exact spend fractions per budget level (72-89% vs 17-45%) across five orchestration policies, and the demonstration that budget is an inert factor because higher levels yield byte-identical episodes rather than merely similar accuracy.
